builder_plan.scenario: Tool errors or unavailable services cause your agent to abandon recoverable tasks.
builder_plan.change: Inject repeatable tool failures and change only the recovery policy.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current retry and fallback behavior under the same injected failures.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Recovered tasks, duplicate side effects, retries, time to recovery, and total cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
summary: The study replaces intuition about guard layers and model choice with a scripted mistake library (22 canonical errors) and engine-native recovery drills across 12 engines and permission/recovery arms, showing damage is governed mainly by engine permissions and undo capability rather than the model. It costs nothing to adopt as knowledge, but operationalizing it means enforcing least-privilege credentials, tested backups, and engine-specific recovery procedures rather than relying on a guard layer whose benefit was not consistently supported. Its conclusions can fail to transfer because the post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected, the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about the guard layer on four engines, and one hypothesis was uninformative because agents never found the credential.
rationale: The paper is a preregistered empirical study of database failure modes and recovery under agent mistakes, not an adoptable method, but its permission-arm and recovery-drill findings directly inform how the reader should configure databases that agents touch.
technique: Empirical audit of agent-caused database damage and recovery

claims.statement: The study replaces intuition about guard layers and model choice with a scripted mistake library (22 canonical errors) and engine-native recovery drills across 12 engines and permission/recovery arms, showing damage is governed mainly by engine permissions and undo capability rather than the model. It costs nothing to adopt as knowledge, but operationalizing it means enforcing least-privilege credentials, tested backups, and engine-specific recovery procedures rather than relying on a guard layer whose benefit was not consistently supported. Its conclusions can fail to transfer because the post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected, the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about the guard layer on four engines, and one hypothesis was uninformative because agents never found the credential.

No quantified performance gain. Empirical finding: engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo; only 3 of 7 preregistered hypotheses (H2 partially, H3, H4) met their decision rule, and some post-hoc results contradict the preregistered outcome for the guard layer G1.
